intro.p1: A sigma protocol is a way to prove “I know a secret” — such as a private key — without showing the secret. Every signature on Ergo is one, and, unlike an ordinary signature, several of them can be glued together into a single proof. This page explains how that works and why it matters.
intro.p2: In Bitcoin, a “signature” is the only cryptographic thing a script can ask for, and combining several signatures (multisig) is done with rather clumsy opcodes. Ergo takes a different route: every cryptographic requirement is a Σ-protocol (sigma protocol), and Σ-protocols can be combined with &&, || and atLeast right inside ErgoScript. That is why the return type of every contract is SigmaProp.

what.title: What is a Σ-protocol?
what.p1: A Σ-protocol is a three-move zero-knowledge proof between a prover and a verifier. The prover wants to show “I know a secret” without revealing the secret:
what.commitment: Commitment: the prover picks a random number and sends a “commitment”.
what.challenge: Challenge: the verifier replies with a random challenge.
what.response: Response: the prover answers with a number that can only be computed by someone who knows the secret.
what.p2: The “there – back – there” shape of these three moves looks like the letter Σ, hence the name. On a blockchain there is nobody to talk back and forth with, so the challenge is replaced by a hash of the message (the transaction) and the commitment — the Fiat–Shamir technique. The result is a non-interactive proof, which is exactly what sits in the spendingProof field of every input.

dlog.title: proveDlog: Schnorr signatures
dlog.p1: The most basic Σ-protocol is proveDlog(h): “I know x such that h = gˣ”. Here g is the generator of the secp256k1 curve, x is the secret key and h is the public key. After applying Fiat–Shamir, this is exactly a Schnorr signature. Every ordinary wallet address (P2PK) is a proveDlog — the 0008cd… tree you’ve already met.
dlog.p2: Play with the toy version below. Change any number — the check still passes, as long as the prover really knows x:
dlog.p3: Why does it work? gᶻ = gr + e·x = gʳ · (gˣ)ᵉ = a · hᵉ. Someone who doesn’t know x would have to predict e in advance to cheat — but e is chosen after the commitment has been sent.
dlog.reuseText: If the same r is used for two different challenges, anyone can solve for x from the two responses. Real wallets generate a fresh r (randomly, or deterministically from the key and message) for every signature.

dh.title: proveDHTuple
dh.p1: The second basic Σ-protocol is proveDHTuple(g, h, u, v): “I know x such that u = gˣ and v = hˣ” — i.e. the quadruple (g, h, u, v) is a Diffie–Hellman tuple. It is the building block for privacy protocols such as ZeroJoin (decentralized mixers) and advanced anonymous signatures, where you need to prove that two values relate to the same secret without revealing it.

combine.title: Combining Σ-protocols: AND, OR, atLeast
combine.p1: The magic is that Σ-protocols can be composed and the result is still a Σ-protocol — still producing a single proof:

or.meaning: One of them signs — the verifier can’t tell which

atLeast.use: Threshold signatures, company wallets, DAO treasuries

ring.title: Ring signatures: signing on behalf of a group
ring.p1: A ring signature says “one of these people signed” without saying who. With alice || bob || carol, the prover only needs to know one secret key.
ring.p2: The trick is in how the other branches are handled. For the branches where the prover does not know the secret, they simulate a proof: pick the challenge and the response first, then compute the commitment backwards so the equation still balances. The real branch is proven normally. Finally, the challenges are tied together so that their XOR equals the overall challenge — that is what stops someone from simulating every branch. Looking at the finished proof, nobody can tell the real branch from the simulated ones, so nobody knows which member of the group signed.

threshold.title: Threshold: k of n
threshold.p1: A threshold signature says “at least k of these n people signed”. atLeast(k, …) uses the same simulation trick: k parties sign for real, the remaining n − k branches are simulated, and the challenges are tied together by a polynomial instead of an XOR (the same idea as Shamir secret sharing). The result is still one proof, and outsiders can’t tell which k parties signed.
threshold.noOpText: In Bitcoin, multisig needs OP_CHECKMULTISIG and reveals the keys of whoever signed. On Ergo, multisig, ring and threshold signatures are just ways of writing an expression — and “who signed” stays private naturally.

tx.title: In a real transaction
tx.p1: When a node validates an input, it does two things:
tx.reduce: Reduces the ErgoTree against the current context: every boolean part (such as HEIGHT > 1000000) is evaluated to true/false. What remains is a pure Σ-protocol tree (or a constant true/false).
tx.verify: Verifies the proof in spendingProof against that Σ-tree, using the transaction bytes as the message.
tx.p2: For example, a miner fee box reduces to true when the transaction has the right shape, so its proof is empty — nobody needs to sign. Read more in ErgoTree & ErgoScript and Transactions.
